articles.title: Singapore built a 350-metre barrage across Marina Channel to create its 15th reservoir in the heart of the city, while using gates and pumps to manage floods and opening the waterfront to recreation
articles.summary: Singapore built Marina Barrage across the mouth of Marina Channel to create a freshwater reservoir in the heart of the city.
articles.body: Singapore built Marina Barrage across the mouth of Marina Channel to create a freshwater reservoir in the heart of the city. The structure was designed to serve three purposes that are controlling floods, supporting the national water supply and providing space for recreation.It created the country’s 15th reservoir and its first in the city centre, while helping expand Singapore’s water catchment area. According to PUB, Singapore’s National Water Agency, Marina Barrage opened in 2008, and Marina Reservoir was commissioned in 2010. The barrage keeps seawater out of the reservoir and helps maintain relatively stable water levels throughout the year.How did Singapore turn Marina Channel into a freshwater reservoirMarina Barrage was built across the mouth of Marina Channel, creating Singapore’s 15th reservoir and the first in the heart of the city. The project was based on the vision of Singapore’s first Prime Minister, the late Lee Kuan Yew, who had envisaged damming the mouth of Marina Channel to create a freshwater reservoir.The barrage spans the 350-metre-wide Marina Channel and acts as a tidal barrier, keeping seawater out of the reservoir. Marina Reservoir was officially commissioned on 20 November 2010 by Lee. Before that, Marina Barrage had been officially opened on 31 October 2008. Desalting began in April 2009, through natural replacement by rainwater, preparing the reservoir to become part of Singapore’s water supply.What role does Marina Barrage play in Singapore’s flood controlThe barrage forms part of a wider flood-control scheme designed to ease flooding in low-lying parts of Singapore. The areas identified by PUB include Chinatown, Boat Quay, Jalan Besar and Geylang.During heavy rain, 9 crest gates can be activated to release excess stormwater into the sea when the tide is low. When the tide is high, giant pumps can drain excess stormwater into the sea instead. These systems allow the barrage to help manage water levels during periods of heavy rainfall.Its flood-control role is one of three main functions identified by PUB, alongside supplying water and providing a venue for recreational and lifestyle activities in the city.Marina Reservoir supports water and recreational activitiesMarina Barrage also provides a setting for water-based activities and public recreation. By removing tidal influence from Marina Reservoir, the structure helps maintain relatively stable water levels throughout the year. These conditions are suitable for activities including kayaking, sailing and dragon boating. The Green Roof has also become a popular destination for visitors.It provides sweeping views of the Singapore skyline and space for activities such as kite-flying and picnicking. These public uses form the third part of the barrage’s stated purpose, alongside flood control and water supply. The site combines water infrastructure with places where people can spend time outdoors, while the reservoir supports a range of activities on the water for visitors and residents.Why is Marina catchment important to Singapore’s water supplyMarina Barrage keeps seawater out of the reservoir, while removing the influence of tides from Marina Reservoir. This allows water levels to remain relatively constant throughout the year. The reservoir has a catchment area of 10,000 hectares, making Marina catchment Singapore’s largest and most urbanised catchment.Together with two other reservoirs, it has increased the country’s water catchment from half to two-thirds of the country’s land area. Marina Reservoir was commissioned as a freshwater reservoir in November 2010, adding to the country’s water supply for future generations. This expanded the area used to collect rainwater.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Government’s anti-cybercrime wing has ‘WhatsApp Web’ warning for you
articles.summary: The government’s anti-cybercrime wing has issued a warning for those who use WhatsApp Web.
articles.body: The government’s anti-cybercrime wing has issued a warning for those who use WhatsApp Web. In a new security advisory issued on Monday (November 23), the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit (NCTAU) under the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) cautioned that active, authenticated WhatsApp Web sessions can be exploited for unauthorised access by hackers by leaving an open door to hijack your account, read private chats and impersonate you to carry out fraud,Once inside, bad actors can read personal messages, view contact lists and group chats, and send messages pretending to be the account owner, leveraging the victim's trusted identity to launch fraud, phishing, and social-engineering scams, the warning explained as per PTI.‘Closing the browser tab is not enough’The I4C specifically stressed that simply closing a browser window or tab does not end a WhatsApp Web session. Users must manually log out every time they finish using the platform on a computer.“Users are therefore advised to exercise caution while using WhatsApp Web, particularly on office computers, shared systems, public computers or devices that may be accessible to other persons," the advisory stated, further warning, “Avoid official or sensitive work on WhatsApp Web. Government, organisational, financial, confidential or other sensitive information should preferably not be exchanged through WhatsApp Web sessions on computers.”Key safety tips from advisoryTo protect accounts from unauthorised takeovers, the I4C recommended the following precautions:Avoid logging into WhatsApp Web on cyber cafe computers, public kiosks, hotel business centers, borrowed laptops or other unknown and public devices.If logging in on a shared system is unavoidable, use the browser’s incognito or private browsing mode but remember to log out manually afterward.Pay close attention to unusual account behaviour, such as unexpected messages sent from your number, strange replies from contacts or any unexplained activity.Keep your devices, operating systems, browsers and security software updated, and steer clear of suspicious downloads, unknown files and cracked software.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: US Democrats to hold 12 presidential primary debates ahead of 2028; candidates must pledge to denounce super PAC spending
articles.summary: The Democratic National Committee reveals plans for 12 debates ahead of the 2028 US presidential election, introducing new eligibility requirements focused on opposing outside political spending.
articles.body: The Democratic National Committee (DNC) has announced plans to organise 12 debates ahead of the 2028 US presidential election, introducing a new eligibility requirement that candidates must publicly oppose certain forms of outside political spending.Under the proposed rules, contenders seeking a place on the debate stage must sign a Fair Campaign Practices Pledge committing them to denounce spending by super PACs and so-called “dark money groups” during the primary campaign. The move follows sustained pressure from progressive Democrats seeking to limit the influence of wealthy donors and outside organisations in party nominations.The debate schedule will begin in June, with the first two events planned for June and July. Five debates are scheduled for 2027, followed by seven in 2028, with the final event expected in March of that year. The DNC previously organised 12 debates during the 2020 presidential primary, the party's most recent open contest for its nomination, according to CNN.The committee said further information, including event dates, venues and media partners, would be released in January. It also plans to announce additional qualification requirements covering polling performance and fundraising.The DNC has appointed a 2028 Debate Planning Committee, led by senior debate adviser Minyon Moore and executive director Roger Lau. Former members of recent presidential campaign teams will also serve on the panel.DNC Chairman Ken Martin said the party wanted to establish a transparent process as it prepared for the next presidential election.In a statement, Martin said the arrangements would help maintain party unity, strengthen its eventual nominee and improve Democrats' chances of winning back the White House.The debate framework also accounts for the possibility of a large number of candidates entering the race. The first events could be spread across two consecutive nights, with participants assigned randomly. Under that arrangement, no more than 20 candidates would be allowed across the two nights combined.The Fair Campaign Practices Pledge is the most significant change to the proposed debate rules. Candidates will have to nominate a representative authorised to raise complaints with the DNC about spending by super PACs or nonprofit organisations registered under Section 501(c)(4) of the US tax code.Such nonprofits are generally not required to disclose their donors publicly, while super PACs can collect and spend unlimited amounts from individuals and corporations, provided they operate independently of candidates' campaigns.If the committee determines that a complaint breaches the pledge's terms, it will ask the relevant candidate to issue a statement condemning the spending. The DNC will also maintain a public online record of complaints and candidates' responses.The arrangement does not give the party the power to stop these organisations from spending money during a primary. The DNC has acknowledged that it lacks the legal authority to impose a blanket ban on super PAC activity. Consequently, outside groups could continue financing campaigns even after a candidate publicly objects to their involvement.Martin has previously said he wanted to address the role of large donors in Democratic primaries. More than a year ago, he introduced a resolution asking the party to examine what measures it could take to limit their influence.The proposal has received backing from several prominent Democrats, including independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, who has repeatedly advocated restrictions on super PAC spending in primary elections.An initial list of supporters shared by a DNC official also included Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Senator Andy Kim of New Jersey, Representative Greg Casar of Texas, Representative Jason Crow of Colorado and former DNC chairman Jaime Harrison.The party's debate rules will also address disputes over the order of state primaries. Candidates could lose their eligibility if they take part in a primary event that has not been authorised by the DNC.The provision could affect New Hampshire, which has a state law requiring it to conduct the country's first presidential primary. Republican Secretary of State David Scanlan has indicated that the state intends to maintain that position.The 2028 nomination process is already changing to the party's early-state schedule. South Carolina will retain its position as the first primary state, while Iowa has been removed. New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia have been added to the early-state lineup as Democrats prepare for a competitive contest to select their next presidential nominee.You use AI every day. articles.title: Telford's Exotic Zoo says sad farewell to Doris the armadillo
articles.summary: Doris was 19 and had been with Telford Exotic Zoo since it opened 15 years ago.
articles.body:
A zoo in Telford has said goodbye to a six-banded armadillo called Doris, who lived to the grand old age of 19, winning a Blue Peter badge and helping to educate thousands of visitors about the rainforest during her long life.

Along with her sibling Dillon, she starred in a short film for the Let's Go Club on CBeebies , and their 19th birthday was marked by BBC Newsround earlier this year.

The pair had been on arthritis medication for some time - Dillon died in June and on Sunday, Telford Exotic Zoo announced Doris "couldn't carry on any more".

Scott Adams, the zoo's managing director, said the pair had lived there since it opened 15 years ago, adding Doris had been "an amazing ambassador".

Doris had come to Telford from another zoo which closed and Adams said she had become very familiar with the staff, regularly walking over to greet them and asking for her head to be rubbed.

The six-banded armadillo is native to South America and Adams said it was unusual for them to live so long.

In the wild they usually live no more than 15 years, although they can live longer in captivity.

In a statement on Facebook at the weekend, the zoo said: "Today she couldn't carry on any more and she went to sleep for the last time at our zoo vets who have helped keep her comfortable in her old age.

The zoo is now in its third location and Doris and Dillon made every move with staff.

They had been the last surviving animals from the day it first opened and the zoo said Doris had "educated and amazed hundreds of thousands of visitors, tens of thousands of school children and inspired them to want to save our amazing rainforests".

Adams said the zoo currently had no other six-banded armadillos, but their "legacy lives on" through its collection of three-banded armadillos, which had welcomed a baby earlier this year.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s foundation gave away nearly $400 million in 2025, but more than $310 million went to another nonprofit he founded; its assets climbed to $16 billion
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s charitable foundation has billions of dollars in assets, but its annual donations remain a relatively small part of that wealth.
articles.body: Elon Musk’s charitable foundation has billions of dollars in assets, but its annual donations remain a relatively small part of that wealth. In 2025, the organisation distributed nearly $400 million, with much of the money directed towards a separate nonprofit established by the billionaire himself. Reportedly, the latest tax filing also offers a glimpse into how the foundation operates, from its limited staffing to Musk’s reported involvement in its activities. While its assets climbed to around $16 billion during the year, the amount distributed was lower than the previous year's record. The figures have renewed attention on where Musk's charitable money goes and how quickly it reaches organisations working outside his own network.The Musk Foundation’s charitable giving fell as its assets climbed to $16 billionThe Musk Foundation distributed close to $400 million in grants during 2025, according to its latest tax return. The filing, first reported by Bloomberg, shows a decline from the $474 million it gave away in 2024, when its charitable distributions reached a record level.Its financial position moved in the opposite direction. The foundation's assets increased by more than $1 billion over the year, reaching approximately $16 billion. An additional $64 million gift of Tesla shares helped boost the foundation's assets. The difference between its accumulated wealth and annual charitable spending is relevant because US private foundations are generally required to meet an annual minimum distribution requirement, calculated using their minimum investment return and certain adjustments.The Musk Foundation has faced questions about its payout levels in the past. Forbes examined its 2024 tax return and reported that it had not met the applicable minimum. However, the rules allow foundations to carry forward certain undistributed amounts and address a shortfall in a subsequent year. The 2025 figures, therefore, need to be considered alongside the foundation's distribution obligations and any eligible carry-forward amounts.How a Musk-founded education nonprofit received the bulk of the foundation’s grantsThe largest share of the foundation's 2025 donations went to The Foundation, a separate nonprofit established by Musk. It received more than $310 million, accounting for over three-quarters of the Musk Foundation's annual giving.The organisation is behind an education project in Bastrop, Texas, near Austin. Its plans centre on a school offering science, technology, engineering and mathematics education at primary and secondary levels. The longer-term ambition is to expand the project into a university.The substantial grant means much of the money distributed by Musk's charitable foundation remained within an organisation connected to his own philanthropic activities, rather than being spread among a wider range of independent charities.The filing also records a $20 million contribution to a donor-advised fund managed by Fidelity Charitable. Musk retains advisory control over the fund, allowing him to recommend where the money should eventually be distributed. Donor-advised funds operate differently from direct charitable grants. Once a contribution is made, the sponsoring organisation has legal control over the assets, while the donor can advise on future distributions. Contributors may also receive a tax deduction when they put money into the fund, subject to applicable rules.Memphis organisations also received millionsOutside the education project and the Fidelity Charitable contribution, several other recipients were based in the Memphis area. The region is also home to large data centre operations associated with Musk's AI business, xAI. Fortune reported Slingshot Memphis, a nonprofit that evaluates poverty-reduction initiatives through research, data and programme assessments, received $5.9 million from the foundation. Regional One Health Foundation was awarded another $9.4 million, with the grant designated for patient care.The donations came as xAI continued developing its Colossus data centre operations in the Memphis area. The company's facilities have been central to its efforts to expand computing capacity for artificial intelligence development.Musk reportedly spends about an hour a week on the foundationDespite its substantial financial resources, the Musk Foundation appears to operate with a very small administrative team. Its tax filing identifies three directors: Musk, Jared Birchall, who oversees the billionaire's family office, and Matilda Simon.Musk is listed as the organisation's president. According to Bloomberg's reporting on the filing, he declared that he spent approximately one hour each week working on foundation-related activities.The limited time commitment stands in contrast to the scale of the organisation's assets and the sums it distributes. The filing, however, does not provide a detailed account of how individual grant decisions are made or how responsibilities are divided among its directors.Musk's Giving Pledge promise and his reported charitable givingMusk signed the Giving Pledge in 2012, promising to donate the majority of his wealth during his lifetime or through his will. The initiative, established by Bill Gates and Melinda French Gates alongside Warren Buffett, invites some of the world's wealthiest individuals to make a public commitment to philanthropy. His reported giving has not kept pace with the increase in his fortune. Bloomberg estimated that Musk donated approximately $1.4 billion between 2021 and 2024. During the same period, his net worth rose by hundreds of billions of dollars.Forbes valued his fortune at around $812 billion on November 21, 2026. Against that estimate, the Musk Foundation's nearly $400 million in 2025 distributions represents roughly 0.05% of his personal wealth. His position on the global wealth rankings has also fluctuated. Musk became the world's first trillionaire in June 2026 following SpaceX's public listing, according to the report, although his estimated fortune has since moved above and below that threshold.Musk has previously spoken about the difficulty of deciding where charitable money should go. He has described giving effectively as a complicated process, saying: “It is very difficult to give money away for the reality of goodness.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'People were screaming in pain', Manchester's Co-op Live gig-goers say
articles.summary: Rap fans say people were "choking" and "coughing up blood" after "some smoke" went off in Co-op Live.
articles.body:
Rap music fans who were evacuated from a concert after an unknown substance was released have said there was a "burning" feeling in their throat and they started to "cough and splutter" and some people were "screaming in pain".

Some 12,000 people were evacuated from Co-op Live Arena after the incident at US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live in Manchester at about 22:00 GMT on Sunday.

One person was taken to hospital, and more than 80 were assessed by paramedics.

Concertgoers have described feeling "unsafe" and seeing "distressing" scenes and people "coughing up blood", with some claiming the venue's security was lax.

Leon Douzi said he was "right next to" where the substance was released, and "there was this gas coming out of a can" and someone holding it and then "it just hit me in the throat" and it felt like "burning", like pepper spray.

He said it was scary and "there was a bit of panic. Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out."

Poppy Rutter and Sophie Billing, both 19, who had travelled from Cambridge to see the concert, said it was not immediately clear what had happened.

Sophie said: "I thought something had gone wrong with smoke coming off stage.

"We started to suffer, coughing and spluttering and feeling tight-chested. A member of staff said it was tear gas.

"Security rushed in and went straight to the pit. We only left as we were starting to feel unsafe and not 100 per cent well."

She said there was "no communication", adding: "You would think Manchester would be extra vigilant, given what's happened in the past."

Joey Howe, a football journalist who was also at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester : "I saw a lot of people streaming out and you go into this panic mode and you see a lot of people running out of the venue.

"The lights have come on and he is being rushed off stage.

The 22-year-old added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking - it was really distressing," Howe said.

"We then decided to leave the venue. It was just really distressing scenes and not something you want to see."

Carol from Bolton, who was sitting in Block 108 of the arena, said: "About 40 minutes into the show, we saw some sort of smoke and a red flare going off.

"Don Toliver left the stage. From where we were sitting, we saw people rushing out of GA (ground access) and security staff wandering around looking lost.

"We sat for a further 45 minutes before finally hearing an announcement at 11pm to leave the arena.

"At no point was there an announcement to evacuate from our level. Very disappointed."

Harper, who was also there, told BBC Radio 5Live: "I was right on the opposite side and I was seeing people cough up blood - I mean, that's when it was really scary for some of us, especially my girlfriend and I.

"I was in shock because I had no idea what was going on because it just stopped and all the lights came on.

"I saw people getting wheelchairs out...I was fearful it was something even worse."

Jessica Moult-Boffey, 23, of Wigan, said she went to the exit and saw "lads on the bridge" which leads into Medlock Square "crying and screaming in pain".

The music fan added that they were "asking for help" but there were only two stewards outside.

She said she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".

"When we went in, no-one checked my bag.

"I held it up and said, 'Do you need to check my bag?'

"The security staff member said: 'No, it's okay.'

"Every single other person I spoke to didn't have their bag checked either."

Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".

It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".

Greater Manchester Police said it was investigating what the substance was and what had caused the incident.

The force said a major incident had been declared after reports of people suffering from the effects of an unknown substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.

Anyone who left the event and has since become unwell is urged to attend their local hospital.

The rapper, whose real name is Caleb Zackery Toliver, was performing at the Manchester venue as part of his Nitrous – Octane world tour.

He is due to perform at London's O2 Arena on Monday, and at Wembley Arena on 24 November.

Last week the 32-year-old musician received five nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards, including for Best New Artist.

He recently released new track TF, which features on the album for blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto VI and on Friday appeared at Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival in Miami alongside Travis Scott.

Toliver has more than six million followers on Instagram. His sixth album, Nitrous, is set to release on 4 December and he is due to appear on US sketch show Saturday Night Live on 5 December.

articles.body: GHAZIABAD: BJP leader Sangeet Som launched a sharp attack on Samajwadi Party leader Azam Khan over his claims of being tortured in jail, saying that the SP leader should fear an encounter as his white kurta was "stained with blood" over his alleged role in the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots."Look, it is only natural for Azam Khan to fear an encounter. Consider how he was responsible for the deaths of innocent people during the Muzaffarnagar riots; his 'white' kurta is not actually white; it is stained with blood. It is a garment that carries the weight of hundreds of lives. Naturally, such an individual should fear an encounter. These people are thugs, mafias; they are hardly leaders," Som said.Som further accused the then Samajwadi Party government of suppressing the actual death toll during the communal violence. He claimed that several people, including followers of the Sanatan tradition, had been killed and that some bodies were never recovered."And let me point out that the Samajwadi Party played a deceptive game back then by suppressing the actual figures. Many people were killed, many followers of the Sanatan tradition, whose bodies were never even recovered. Such atrocities took place there, all at the behest of Azam Khan," he alleged.Taking his criticism further, Som urged Khan to join SP president Akhilesh Yadav on his proposed December 12 visit to Ayodhya and seek forgiveness at the Ram temple for his alleged opposition to its construction."I have one piece of advice for him: since Akhilesh Yadav is planning to visit Ayodhya for a pilgrimage on December 12, Azam Khan should accompany him. He should take a dip in the Saryu River, apply a tilak, and prostrate himself at the feet of Lord Ram to seek forgiveness. After all, he was part of the very committee that opposed the construction of the temple for Lord Ram," he said.Som added that seeking forgiveness could be a first step towards atoning for what he described as Khan's past actions.Reacting to Akhilesh Yadav's use of religious greetings such as 'Ram-Ram' and 'Radhe-Radhe', Som compared the SP leader to Kalnemi, a demon from the Ramayana known for deception. He alleged that Yadav was opposed to the Sanatan tradition despite publicly invoking religious expressions."Look, Akhilesh Yadav is like Kalnemi. He acts one way during the day and another at night, chanting 'Ram, Ram' while hiding under a blanket. He is fundamentally opposed to the Sanatan tradition; he has never liked it," Som said.The BJP leader also questioned Yadav's decision to visit Ayodhya on December 12, arguing that December 6 would have been a more appropriate date. He referred to the 1990 police firing on kar sevaks during the tenure of the then Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Mulayam Singh Yadav, Akhilesh Yadav's father."And, as a matter of fact, he chose the wrong day. It would have been better if he had chosen December 6th, the day his father committed that grave sin by ordering gunfire on unarmed kar sevaks, leading to the deaths of hundreds. I would advise Akhilesh Yadav to visit on December 6th instead. That way, at least, there might be some form of atonement," he said.Som also criticised Akhilesh Yadav's promise to reopen primary schools that were allegedly shut down over the past decade if the Samajwadi Party returned to power. He accused the former chief minister of promoting lawlessness and claimed that an SP government would embolden criminals, release terrorists from prison and encourage communal tensions.He further alleged that Yadav's supporters were intimidating people during his roadshows by hitting them with vehicles."Even now, look at his roadshows: his supporters are already hitting people with their vehicles. They have begun their reign of terror and are acting in a way that creates an atmosphere of fear among the people of the state," he said.Referring to gangsters and politicians Atiq Ahmed and Mukhtar Ansari, Som asserted that criminal elements would no longer be able to exercise influence and accused the SP leadership of depending on mafia figures for electoral support."But given how figures like Atiq and Mukhtar have been reduced to dust, no mafia don will be able to stand tall again. Akhilesh Yadav, you can no longer win elections by relying on the mafia," he said.Som also responded to Akhilesh Yadav's recent remarks about perfume shops allegedly being replaced by outlets selling 'gomutra' (cow urine). Defending the use of cow urine, he claimed it had medicinal properties and was used in treatments for various illnesses, including cancer.Taking another dig at the SP chief, Som suggested that consuming cow urine before visiting Ayodhya could help address what he described as Yadav's mental condition."Look, the entire population of the country likes cow urine, and it is used for medical treatment -- even for conditions like cancer; it is used to treat people across the country. If Akhilesh Yadav were to drink some cow urine before going to seek the blessings of Lord Ram, perhaps his own mind might get some effective treatment too," Som said.Meanwhile, Azam Khan returned to his residence in Rampur on Wednesday evening after being released from Dasna District Jail in Ghaziabad. His release followed interim bail granted by the court. articles.title: Microsoft CFO Amy Hood, who was rejected twice and later joined the company without knowing salary, has advice for Gen Z: ‘I can’t believe I’m saying this but …’
articles.summary: Amy Hood, the chief financial officer (CFO) of Microsoft, did not have a master plan for her career.
articles.body: Amy Hood, the chief financial officer (CFO) of Microsoft, did not have a master plan for her career. As an economics undergraduate at Duke University in the 1990s, she could not have guessed she would one day hold the top finance job at one of the world’s biggest tech companies. For Hood, her career has looked more like a roller coaster than a ladder. That is the lesson she shared with the class of 2026 at Duke’s commencement ceremony. Her lesson comes at a delicate time when the tech industry is undergoing a transformation, and companies across the tech industry, Microsoft included, have cut thousands of roles in recent years as they restructure and invest more in artificial intelligence (AI).How Amy Hood’s career took shapeHood graduated from Duke in 1994. She built her early career at Goldman Sachs and later earned an MBA from Harvard. Over time, she realised corporate banking was not how she wanted to spend the rest of her life. So she quit, without much of a plan for what came next. She told students in May: “As you start out, many successful careers are rarely—if ever—a straight line. Your next step doesn’t have to be a perfect one. It just has to be an opportunity.”She found what seemed like the perfect reset: an internship with the National Park Service.“I thought, this is perfect. It’s a sign—I’ll get assigned to Yosemite or Yellowstone, someplace iconic. I’ll work outdoors, I’ll live somewhere beautiful, and feel the space and energy that nature provides,” Hood recalled. Instead, the then 30-year-old was sent to Alcatraz Island, which she described as “a prison on a rock”. It was nothing like what she had imagined, and she quit after a single day.Microsoft rejected her twiceMonths later, after a long job search, a friend called and asked if she wanted to interview at Microsoft. She had already been rejected by the company twice. This time she landed a role in investor relations and accepted the offer without even asking about the salary. The gamble still paid off. Over the next decade, she rose steadily through the ranks and was named CFO in 2013.Why her advice matters for today’s graduatesFor many of today’s graduates, Hood’s winding road to the top may feel out of reach. Expectations are also out of step with the job market. Hood acknowledged the uncertainty facing Gen Z, however, she argued that many young workers are better prepared than they think. In her view, the bigger challenge is letting go of the idea that they must have everything figured out right away.“I can’t believe I’m saying this to some of the most accomplished young people on the planet, but maybe lower your bar a little. Be open that something may not be exactly right, but could turn out to be a perfect place to learn about yourself—what you like, what you don’t. All the steps matter, and it took me decades to figure that out,” she said.She also urged graduates to stay adaptable and curious in a world that is changing faster than it did for any earlier generation.“You will figure out who you are by stepping in and letting people push back, by doing things that scare you just a little, by raising your hand when you’re pretty sure you don’t have the right answer, and by taking a job that doesn’t make sense on paper but makes sense to you,” she told graduates.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Jeff Bezos made two big donations in 2026, what makes the stock gifts 'historic' is that both go to the Day 1 of ...
articles.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has donated more than $600 million worth of Amazon shares in 2026, but two of his most recent gifts stand out for a unique
articles.body: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has donated more than $600 million worth of Amazon shares in 2026, but two of his most recent gifts stand out for a unique reason: some of the stock was acquired on Julu 5, 1994, the day he incorporated the company that would eventually become Amazon. According to a report by Fortune, the shares effectively date back to the company’s ‘Day 1’, making them among the earliest Amazon shares still linked to Bezos’ holdings. The Amazon founder and executive chair donated 674,088 shares on Nov. 12 and 97,404 more the next day, according to a Nov. 16 SEC filing. Forbes valued the 771,492 shares at $198.9 million, based on Amazon’s $257.75 close that day.Jeff Bezos donated nearly $200 million donated in NovemberAccording to securities filings cited by Fortune, Bezos donated 674,088 Amazon shares on November 12 and another 97,404 shares on November 13. Based on Amazon's closing share price of $257.75 on November 16, Forbes estimated the value of the combined 771,492 shares at roughly $198.9 million.Part of the donation, worth about $25 million, went to the Bezos Earth Fund. The fund also filed notice of its intention to sell the shares, according to SEC filings.What makes this particular donation noteworthy is that the shares were originally acquired on July 5, 1994, the same day Bezos incorporated the company that later became Amazon, nearly three years before the retailer's public market debut in 1997.Where the shares wentThe smaller gift, worth about $25 million, went to the Bezos Earth Fund Foundation, which Bezos founded. It filed a notice of its intent to sell the shares. Bezos acquired those shares on July 5, 1994, the day he incorporated the company that became Amazon, almost three years before its 1997 IPO. The filings don’t name the recipient of the larger gift. The November gifts follow two earlier rounds: more than 1.25 million shares in May and 415,580 in August, worth about $323 million and $107 million at the Nov. 16 close. In all, Bezos has donated at least 2.44 million shares this year, worth about $629.1 million at that price.Day 1 Academies, the nonprofit behind his network of tuition-free preschools, received at least 450,837 of those shares, 220,200 in May and 230,637 in August. With the Earth Fund, the two nonprofits he founded account for about 22.5% of this year’s donated shares. The filings describe the rest only as gifts to nonprofits. Even after the donations, Bezos directly held more than 878 million Amazon shares, worth about $226.4 billion per Forbes, so this year’s gifts are under 0.3% of the stake.More than $600 million worth of stock donated this yearThe November transactions add to two earlier rounds of charitable stock gifts made by Bezos in 2026. Fortune reported that he donated more than 1.25 million Amazon shares in May and another 415,580 shares in August. Using Amazon's November 16 closing price, those donations were valued at approximately $323 million and $107 million respectively.Altogether, the Amazon founder has donated at least 2.44 million Amazon shares this year, worth about $629 million based on the same valuation.A deadline approachingBezos launched the Earth Fund in 2020 with a pledge to give away $10 billion by 2030. As of late September it had granted about $2.4 billion, meaning it would need to average roughly $1.8 billion a year to meet the goal, Fortune reported. On Nov. 19, the fund told Fortune it is committing more than $100 million to protect the Amazon rainforest through 15 new grants across South America. Day 1 Academies runs 38 Montessori-inspired preschools in underserved communities across six states and enrolled 2,456 students for 2026-27. They grew out of a $2 billion commitment Bezos announced in 2018, whose other arm, the Day 1 Families Fund, awarded $102.5 million to 32 groups in 2025.What the Day 1 network doesDay 1 Academies operates 38 tuition-free preschools across Arizona, Florida, Hawaii, Kentucky, Texas and Washington. According to its annual report, the network enrolled 2,456 students for the 2026-27 academic year. The schools were created through the Day 1 Fund, a $2 billion philanthropic commitment announced by Bezos in 2018 to support early childhood education and families experiencing homelessness. Another arm of the initiative, the Day 1 Families Fund, provides grants to organisations helping families move from homelessness into stable housing.How his giving compares to his ex-wife MacKenzie ScottBezos and his wife, Lauren Sánchez Bezos, had given an estimated $4.7 billion through the end of 2025, 10th on Forbes’ list of top US philanthropists, with about $600 million of it in 2025. Bezos has said he plans to give away most of his fortune in his lifetime. He told CNN in 2022 that the hard part is working out how to do it “in a levered way.” His ex-wife, MacKenzie Scott, gave away $7.2 billion in 2025 alone, bringing her total since their 2019 divorce to $26.4 billion, Forbes estimates. That one year exceeded what Bezos and Sánchez Bezos have given in their lifetimes.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.summary: Telangana HC pulls up govt for inaction on DSC-2002 eligible candidates, questions repeated assurances, finds affidavits flawed; principal secretary to attend Nov 30.
articles.body: Hyderabad: Taking a serious view of years of inaction on the claims of candidates found eligible for selection under DSC-2002, Telangana High Court questioned the state govt over repeatedly telling the court that their cases were under consideration without taking a concrete decision.A bench of Acting Chief Justice P Sam Koshy and Justice NV Shravan Kumar made the observations while hearing a contempt case filed by six aspirants.Following earlier directions, Yogita Rana, principal secretary, school education department, appeared before the court and apprised it of developments in the matter, including additional affidavits filed by the department.After examining the affidavits, the bench observed that those filed in the contempt cases concerning DSC-2002 appointments were neither proper nor justifiable. It also found the affidavits incorrect with regard to petitioners from Nizamabad and Karimnagar districts.Observing that officials appeared to be misleading counsel appearing before the court, the bench noted that govt had repeatedly submitted in 2022 and 2024 that the candidates’ representations and recommendations made by district educational officers (DEOs) were being examined and appropriate decisions would be taken.Despite those assurances, no concrete action had followed for years. “The state had raised hopes among the candidates by making such submissions and later expressed helplessness over their claims,” the court remarked.Special govt pleader S Rahul Reddy sought one week to enable the state govt to take remedial steps and pass appropriate orders in the cases of two petitioners.In the case of the remaining four petitioners, he submitted that no recommendations had been made in their favour by the DEOs of the erstwhile Medak and Warangal districts.Counsel for the petitioners disputed the submission, maintaining that the respective DEOs had also made recommendations in their cases. articles.title: Not an alliance, but a strategic web: How India and Japan are tightening the net on China
articles.summary: India and Japan sit on opposite sides of China, separated by the vast expanse of its landmass.
articles.body: India and Japan sit on opposite sides of China, separated by the vast expanse of its landmass. Yet an increasingly assertive and expansionist Beijing has given both countries a common strategic challenge. Each is independently building military capabilities and investing in defence preparedness to deter China from pursuing its territorial ambitions. Though geographically distant from each other, New Delhi and Tokyo are united by a shared apprehension: that China's growing military power could threaten their territorial integrity and undermine the regional balance.Now, the two countries are taking their cooperation a step further. On November 19, at the fourth India-Japan 2+2 meeting of foreign and defence ministers in Tokyo, the two sides signed a Letter of Intent that will allow Japanese forces to use Indian military ranges for live-fire exercises for the first time, including firing missiles. It is perhaps the clearest indication yet that the India-Japan strategic partnership is moving beyond diplomatic declarations and into tangible military cooperation.Why the two countries are drawing closerChina's military modernisation, expanding naval presence, long-range missile capabilities and increasingly assertive territorial claims have reshaped the Indo-Pacific security landscape. India and Japan experience this pressure in different theatres, but face a common strategic challenge.For India, the pressure is concentrated along the Himalayan frontier, particularly since the 2020 Galwan Valley clash and the subsequent military standoff in eastern Ladakh. Chinese military deployments, expanded airfields and missile capabilities in Tibet and Xinjiang, coupled with Beijing's close military partnership with Pakistan, have created the prospect of a two-front challenge for New Delhi.For Japan, the concerns are centred on the maritime domain and the islands of the western Pacific. Chinese Coast Guard vessels operate regularly around the Senkaku Islands, administered by Japan but claimed by China as the Diaoyu Islands. Tokyo is also increasingly concerned about Chinese military activity around Taiwan, which lies close to Japan's southwestern island chain.The geography may be different, but the underlying challenge is the same: a stronger China increasingly willing to use its military weight and strategic influence to advance its interests. Neither government describes the partnership as an alliance directed against Beijing. Both instead emphasise their commitment to a free, open and rules-based Indo-Pacific. Yet their efforts to deepen interoperability, logistics, maritime surveillance and defence-industrial cooperation have an unmistakable deterrent dimension: strengthening their own capabilities while raising the costs of any attempt to alter the regional status quo by force.How the relationship was builtIndia-Japan ties have historical roots stretching back to the sixth century, but their security dimension is relatively recent. The two countries signed a peace treaty and established diplomatic relations on April 28, 1952. A Global Partnership followed in 2000, which was elevated to a Strategic and Global Partnership in 2006.The Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation, signed in October 2008, provided the first formal framework for defence exchanges, maritime security and counterterrorism cooperation. In September 2014, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe elevated the relationship to a Special Strategic and Global Partnership.A series of agreements subsequently gave this partnership greater institutional and operational depth. A 2014 memorandum provided for defence exchanges and training, while two agreements signed in 2015 covered defence equipment and technology transfer, and the protection of classified military information.In 2018, an arrangement between the Indian Navy and the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF) further strengthened naval cooperation. One of the most consequential agreements has been the Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement (ACSA), signed on September 9, 2020, and brought into force on July 11, 2021. It allows the two militaries to provide each other with supplies and services, including fuel, food, transportation, maintenance and medical support. This logistical framework makes prolonged exercises and military deployments considerably easier.The maritime coreMaritime security remains the area where India's and Japan's strategic interests overlap most directly. Both countries depend heavily on uninterrupted shipping through the Indian Ocean and the Malacca Strait, while keeping a close watch on China's expanding naval presence, submarine deployments and network of port facilities across the region.On August 20, during Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi's visit to New Delhi, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and Koizumi signed a Memorandum of Arrangement on Maritime Security Cooperation.The agreement provides for greater information-sharing on maritime domain awareness, search and rescue, disaster relief, the protection of sea lines of communication, ship visits and logistics support. It also covers mine countermeasures, joint naval design and shipbuilding, and the use of each other's shipyards for repairs.A working group at the level of Joint Secretary or Director General will oversee its implementation. The November 19 meeting in Tokyo reaffirmed the importance of this framework and the need to take the cooperation forward.Training togetherJoint military exercises are the most visible manifestation of the growing relationship. They also provide an opportunity for the two forces to familiarise themselves with each other's operating procedures, tactics and equipment.Dharma Guardian, the annual exercise between the Indian Army and the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force, has been held since 2018, alternating between the two countries. Its seventh edition took place from February 24 to March 9 at Chaubattia in Uttarakhand, with 120 personnel from each side. Japan deployed troops from its 32nd Infantry Regiment, while India was represented by the Ladakh Scouts. The exercise focused on counterterrorism operations and combat in semi-urban environments.At sea, the bilateral naval exercise JIMEX, now referred to as JAIMEX in official statements, began in 2012. It covers a range of operational areas, including anti-submarine and surface warfare, air defence, maritime surveillance and search and rescue.Air force cooperation has also gained momentum. The first Veer Guardian exercise was held in January 2023 at Hyakuri Air Base in Japan, with Indian Su-30MKI fighters operating alongside Japanese F-2 and F-15 aircraft. Veer Guardian 26, scheduled for this year, will mark another milestone, with Japanese Air Self-Defense Force fighters visiting India for the first time.Both countries also participate in the multilateral Malabar naval exercise. Originally launched as an India-US exercise in 1992, it became a permanent four-nation engagement with Japan joining in 2015 and Australia returning in 2020, completing the Quad format. This year, INS Sahyadri and JS Mogami participated in Malabar 2026 off the Japanese coast.The live-fire stepThe Letter of Intent signed in Tokyo marks a significant expansion of this military cooperation. It opens the way for Japan's Self-Defense Forces to conduct live-fire training at Indian firing ranges, including exercises involving surface-to-ship missiles.For Japan, which has limited space at home for large-scale missile training, access to Indian ranges would offer valuable additional room to train. For India, the arrangement demonstrates a degree of strategic trust and allows it to extend its military infrastructure to a key partner.However, the distinction between intent and implementation is important. The document is a Letter of Intent, and the two defence establishments have been asked to expedite the necessary arrangements. It does not mean Japanese missile units have already fired weapons in India, or that Japan has been granted unrestricted access to Indian military ranges. The precise scope, procedures and modalities of the arrangement still need to be worked out.Nevertheless, the significance is hard to miss. Cooperation that was once largely confined to dialogue, port visits and joint exercises is now moving towards more substantive military access and training arrangements.From exercises to industryPerhaps the more consequential development is the growing emphasis on joint defence technology and industrial cooperation. The clearest example is UNICORN, an integrated communications antenna mast developed by Japan. Instead of having several separate antennas on a warship, the system consolidates them into a single structure, reducing electromagnetic interference and the vessel's radar signature.In November 2024, the two countries signed a Memorandum of Implementation to co-develop UNICORN masts for Indian Navy warships, with Bharat Electronics Limited working alongside Japanese partners. Following the Tokyo meeting, the joint statement said India expects acceptance of necessity for the related arrangements by February 2027. This indicates that the project is progressing through the acquisition process, although the system is not yet in service.The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Japan's Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency (ATLA) are also expected to begin joint research on missiles and other advanced technologies. Robotics and unmanned ground vehicles have emerged as additional areas of interest, although publicly available information does not yet indicate a fully established joint development programme in these fields.Japan's gradual relaxation of its defence equipment and technology transfer restrictions has helped create opportunities for such cooperation. India, meanwhile, offers a large defence market, manufacturing capacity and the possibility of developing production partnerships that extend beyond the two countries."At the fourth India-Japan 2+2 Foreign and Defence Ministerial Meeting in Tokyo on 19 November 2026, the two sides signed a Letter of Intent enabling Japan’s Self-Defence Forces to conduct live-fire training on Indian ranges for the first time, including surface-to-ship missiles developed to counter Chinese maritime pressure," Sriparna Pathak, professor of China Studies, and the founding Director of the Centre for Northeast Asian Studies at O.P. Jindal Global University, told TOI."India and Japan simultaneously agreed to accelerate cooperation in underwater, missile and niche technologies, finalise reciprocal naval ship-repair access, and advance transfer of Japan’s UNICORN stealth antenna system to the Indian Navy under the 'Design with Japan, Make in India' framework. These steps build on the August 2026 Memorandum of Arrangement on Maritime Security Cooperation, which is now being translated into practical collaboration on maritime and air domain awareness, mine countermeasures and information sharing between the Indian Navy and Japan Maritime Self-Defence Force. India and Japan’s rapidly maturing partnership is forcing Beijing to reassess its room for manoeuvre across the Indo-Pacific by combining operational military depth with economic de-risking. They simultaneously agreed to accelerate cooperation in underwater, missile and niche technologies, finalise reciprocal naval ship-repair access, and advance transfer of Japan’s UNICORN stealth antenna system to the Indian Navy under the 'Design with Japan, Make in India' framework."Partnership, not allianceDespite the growing scope of cooperation, India and Japan remain some distance away from a formal military alliance. Neither has a mutual defence treaty obligating it to come to the other's aid in the event of an attack. India continues to place a premium on strategic autonomy, while Japan's postwar pacifist Constitution, particularly Article 9, continues to shape the limits and character of its military role.Their threat perceptions, too, are not identical. India's primary security concerns lie along the Himalayan frontier and across the Indian Ocean, while Japan's are concentrated in the East China Sea, around Taiwan and across the western Pacific. Both countries also maintain substantial economic ties with China. There is no joint military command or integrated operational plan between them.What they are building instead is a strategic network rather than an alliance. Greater maritime awareness, reciprocal logistics support, regular military exercises, defence technology partnerships and cooperation through the Quad are gradually creating a more interconnected security architecture in the Indo-Pacific.The objective is not necessarily to confront China militarily, but to make coercion more difficult and costly. By strengthening their individual capabilities and expanding the areas in which they can work together, India and Japan are seeking to deter Beijing without committing themselves to an automatic military response.How far this partnership ultimately goes will depend on whether the political understanding, military exercises and technology agreements translate into sustained operational capabilities. For now, however, the direction is unmistakable: India and Japan are building a strategic web that could significantly complicate China's calculations across the Indo-Pacific.

articles.title: ‘Nothing to do with politics’: Waris Punjab De after Warring visits Amritpal family
articles.summary: Congress MP Raja Warring visited Amritpal Singh’s family in Jallupur Khera for his grandmother’s Bhog; Amritpal joined via video link, Waris Punjab De says non-political.
articles.body: Jallupur Khera: Punjab Congress former chief and Ludhiana MP Amrinder Singh Raja Warring visited Jallupur Khera on Monday to offer condolences to the family of jailed Khadoor Sahib MP and Akali Dal Waris Punjab De chief Amritpal Singh during the Bhog and Antim Ardas for his grandmother Charan Kaur. Amritpal joined the proceedings through video conferencing, as permitted by the court.Warring’s visit comes amid an organisational reshuffle in the Congress following his recent removal as Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee (PPCC) president. It has also drawn attention against the backdrop of changing political equations ahead of the 2027 assembly elections.Waris Punjab De spokesperson Shamsher Singh Padhri said paying respects to elders and sharing the grief of a bereaved family was a longstanding tradition in Punjab, irrespective of political affiliations.Asked about Warring’s meeting with Amritpal’s father, Tarsem Singh, Padhri said the Congress MP had met the family to convey his condolences. “His visit was purely personal and had nothing to do with politics,” he said.Political analyst Jagdeep Singh said Punjab’s political culture had traditionally allowed leaders across party lines to stand with families during bereavement. However, he cautioned against reading too much into the meeting at this stage.“While such visits are often rooted in social courtesy and respect, they can also acquire political significance, particularly when made against the backdrop of changing political equations. articles.title: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia’s CEO, president and board director: Read company's full statement
articles.summary: Nvidia announced on Monday (November 23) that co-founder Jensen Huang has been reinstated as president, chief executive officer (CEO), and a member of its
articles.body: Nvidia announced on Monday (November 23) that co-founder Jensen Huang has been reinstated as president, chief executive officer (CEO), and a member of its Board of Directors, effective immediately. In the announcement, the chipmaker stated that its Board voted unanimously to bring Huang back following a series of meetings and discussions that satisfied directors regarding his candor and ability to lead. While reaching its decision, the Board also consulted with senior levels of the US government, concluding based on that input that Huang’s return poses no national security risk.Read Nvidia’s full statement on reinstating Jensen Huang as company CEONvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: England's tearaway quick bowler reinvented as a top-order batter
articles.summary: Katie George was once a tearaway fast bowler but, after years of injury pain, tells BBC Sport about reinventing herself as a top-order batter.
articles.body:
Sportspeople are faced with a question when injuries hit again and again. Do I try one more time or should I walk away?

England's Katie George came really close to choosing the latter option last year.

"I had a couple of conversations with my close family and partner about whether it was taking too much out of me and whether I was happy with the person I was," she says. "I was pretty miserable."

George made her England debut in 2018 aged 18 as a tearaway fast bowler. She was quick. Some coaches believed generationally so.

She played seven internationals between March and July before the injuries first hit that summer. George is matter of fact about how many have followed. The list is enough to make the rest of us wince.

"Nine stress fractures in my back," she says. "I tore the cartilage off my rib.

"Bits and bobs. Ankle surgery. I have missed a lot of cricket."

Unable to bowl because of her back and little more than a tailender with the bat, George got into sides purely for her athleticism and a penchant for stunning catches. She was occasionally referred to as a 'specialist fielder'.

The label was meant as a compliment, but it still stung. She says she felt like an "empty uniform".

"For a long time I was worried about being the [injury prone ex-Liverpool and England striker] Daniel Sturridge - what could have been, all of that talent wasted," says George, who played football for Portsmouth in her youth.

"I found that really difficult. I didn't want to be that person.

"Over a period of time you get told you are really resilient and you have been through so much. Then when it keeps happening there is pressure and it gets harder.

"You need to look brave and be resilient and show less emotion than you are feeling. Anyone knows when you bottle that up it can get quite tricky."

Then came George's end-of-year appraisal at Warwickshire - that uncomfortable question. Quit or change something. George opted the latter.

Alongside coach Ali Maiden, an unlikely plan was hatched. George had more ducks than fifties at that point in her professional career but why not try and build on flashes of potential. Why not try and become a frontline batter?

"I always knew I was half decent at bowling but I never had that feeling for batting," she says.

"Right the way through age groups and my first fifty at Western Storm, there were moments where in a game it would come off but I would have no idea how to replicate it.

"I would always put it down to a fluke."

The turnaround has been extraordinary. Batting most regularly at number three, George topped the average tables for this season's One-Day Cup with a figure of 77.55.

A 98 against Blaze in April was followed by a first professional century against Lancashire in June. An unbeaten ton against Durham rounded off the campaign. She even opened in the T20 Blast.

"It is crazy it happened but there was a lot of hard work and I am very grateful to Ali," she says.

"He pushed me and challenged me as to why couldn't I change the narrative a little bit. I want to impact games.

"I don't want to sit on the bench. I can do that from my sofa."

As a result, George will travel to India for an England A tour that begins later this month.

She is there alongside youngsters tipped for bright futures but also established names like Lauren Filer and Tilly Corteen-Colman. Her partner Issy Wong was named in the squads but has withdrawn because of injury.

"We were doing a team thing a couple of weeks ago and we were asked what we are most proud of," George says.

"Until the last few months it probably would have been my England debut but, once I thought about it, it was actually being stood in that team room as a batter and wearing this kit again.

"If you said I would be here as a batter in England kit I would definitely have laughed and said you were smoking something."

Given her past, George would be wise not to look too far into the future. She has not given up on bowling again regularly, nor is she ready to listen to advice to stop.

Instead, she has been named Warwickshire captain for next season so will at least have the option to decide herself when to bowl.

Before then, England coach Charlotte Edwards, selector Lydia Greenway and England's new managing director of women's cricket Leah Poulton will all be in India for the upcoming tour, providing George the chance to impress.

"My dream would be to play a red-ball game for England," she says. "That is what I set out for do.

"It is what I watched as a kid with my dad. I vividly remember my first ever Test match watching Jimmy Anderson running in and bowling.

"Whether I am able to, I don't know. Maybe it will be as a batter - that would be the biggest plot twist ever."
